templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. Before starting a routine task, you notice a spill beside the walkway. No one has fallen, but people could step in it.
templates.prompt: What is the best next step?

options.text: Pause nearby work and alert your {lead} to the spill.
options.why: The spill is an immediate hazard. Pausing nearby work and alerting the responsible person helps prevent someone from slipping.

options.text: Step over the spill and finish your task before mentioning it.
options.why: People could still walk into the spill while you work, so delaying the warning leaves the hazard in place.
options.misconception: A hazard can wait when no one has fallen yet.

options.text: Ask a coworker to watch the spill while you continue working nearby.
options.why: A warning from one coworker does not make the area safe for everyone who may pass through.
options.misconception: One person's informal warning is enough to control a hazard.

options.text: Clean it up immediately without checking the workplace procedure or asking for help.
options.why: The spill's contents and the correct cleanup process are not stated. Follow the workplace procedure and involve the responsible person.
options.misconception: Any spill is safe to clean without checking what it contains.

templates.principle: Pause when you identify a hazard, protect people from exposure, and report it through the stated workplace process.

review.notes: The scenario does not identify the spill contents, so the best response is to prevent exposure and alert the lead rather than assume a cleanup method.

templates.timing: The hazard should be controlled before routine work continues.

templates.scenario: While working as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you notice {hazard}. It is not a fire or other emergency that calls for evacuation.
templates.prompt: Arrange these actions in the order you would take them.

steps.text: Stop work in that area and stay clear of the hazard yourself
Warn nearby coworkers so no one walks into it
Tell your {lead} about the hazard right away
Follow your {lead}'s instructions for dealing with it
Go back to your task once the area has been made safe

precedence.why: Continuing to work near a hazard puts you at risk, so stop before you do anything else.
Stopping first keeps you from being hurt while you find and tell the right person.
You cannot follow instructions that have not been given yet.
Work should resume only after the hazard has been dealt with the way your lead directs.
Coworkers need to know about the hazard before everyone goes back to work around it.

templates.principle: Make yourself and others safe first, report the hazard to the person responsible, and return to work only once it has been handled.

review.notes: Explicitly excludes fire/evacuation emergencies. Warning coworkers and reporting may happen in either order; both alternates are professionally sound. No step asks the student to fix the hazard themselves.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {coworker} asks you to initial {task|the} to show the {equipment} was inspected today. The inspection has not been done. {coworker} says, "We're behind, and it was fine yesterday." Your workplace requires each check to be completed before it is signed off, and your {lead} is on site.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Decline to initial it, and tell your {lead} the check has not been done so it can be scheduled.
options.why: Signing for a check that was not done creates a false record and could hide a real problem. Telling your {lead} gets the inspection scheduled by the person who can fit it in.

options.text: Initial it, since {coworker} has more experience and says the {equipment} was fine yesterday.
options.why: Yesterday's condition does not show today's. Equipment can change between uses, which is why the check exists.
options.misconception: A coworker's experience or past results can replace the actual check.

options.text: Initial it now and do the check later in the day, so that the record is accurate by closing time.
options.why: Signing before the work is done makes the record untrue in the meantime, and anyone relying on it during the day is relying on a check that has not happened.
options.misconception: Signing early is fine as long as the work eventually gets done.

options.text: Decline to initial it and ask {coworker} to make sure the check is done before the shift ends.
options.why: Declining is right, but a missed check is a safety gap that your {lead} should know about. Leaving it between coworkers risks the check being skipped again.
options.misconception: Handling it between coworkers is enough.

templates.principle: Sign off only on checks that have actually been done, and take schedule problems to the person who can solve them instead of recording work that did not happen.

review.notes: Workplace rule stated in scenario. Best action does not ask the student to perform the inspection, only to decline and escalate. Acceptable option declines correctly but skips escalation.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. A posted sign says safety glasses must be worn for part of {task|the}. Yours keep fogging up, and the part of the task that needs them takes only a couple of minutes.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Wear the glasses for that part, and tell your {lead} about the fogging so you can get a better fit.
options.why: The sign calls for protection during that part of the task. Reporting the fogging gets you a pair that works.

options.text: Skip the glasses since it is only a couple of minutes, and be extra careful instead.
options.why: An eye injury can happen in seconds. Being careful does not replace protection that the sign requires.
options.misconception: A short task does not need protection.

options.text: Wear the glasses pushed up on your forehead, so you have them on you if you need them.
options.why: Glasses on your forehead do not protect your eyes, even if they look like you are following the sign.
options.misconception: Having the equipment nearby counts as using it.

options.text: Ask a coworker to keep watch for trouble while you do that part without the glasses on.
options.why: A lookout cannot stop something from reaching your eyes. The protection has to be on you during the task.
options.misconception: Another person watching is the same as protection.

templates.principle: Wear required protective equipment for the whole task, and report problems with fit so you can get something that works.

review.notes: Posted sign stated in scenario; no claims about regulations.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. The fire alarm sounds while you are in the middle of helping {client|a} with {document|a}. Posted instructions tell employees to use the closest marked exit when the alarm sounds.

options.text: Stop what you are doing and head out by the exit route nearest you, helping others who need directions.
options.why: The posted instructions point employees to the closest marked exit. Stopping right away is more important than finishing any task.

options.text: Finish what you are doing so that nothing is left in a mess, and leave after that.
options.why: No task is worth the delay in an alarm. Work can be picked up later, but time spent finishing cannot be recovered.
options.misconception: Finishing the task first is more responsible.

options.text: Go to your locker to get your belongings before heading to the exit.
options.why: Collecting belongings costs time and may take you away from the exit route. Personal items can be replaced.
options.misconception: I should not leave my things behind.

options.text: Walk around to find where the alarm is coming from, so you can tell others what is happening.
options.why: Searching for the source puts you at risk and delays leaving. Trained responders will handle that.

templates.principle: When an alarm sounds, stop and leave by the posted route right away; belongings and unfinished work can wait.

review.notes: Posted instruction stated in scenario; no specific procedures claimed.

templates.timing: An alarm is sounding, so leaving comes before any task or errand.

templates.scenario: An evacuation is called at {workplace|the}. Your workplace has posted evacuation instructions.
templates.prompt: Put these actions in the order you would take them.

steps.text: Stop work and leave equipment the way you were trained to
Leave by the nearest marked exit
Check in with the person taking attendance

precedence.why: Leaving equipment safely first prevents it from becoming a hazard while people evacuate.
You cannot reach the meeting point without first leaving the building.
Attendance is taken at the meeting point.

templates.principle: In an evacuation, secure your work as trained, leave by the marked route, assemble, and check in.

review.notes: Posted instructions stated; no specific legal requirements.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You find an unlabeled spray bottle in the supply area. {coworker} says, "It is just cleaner, go ahead and use it." Your workplace keeps safety data sheets for every approved product.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Do not use it, and tell your {lead} so it can be identified using labels and the safety data sheets.
options.why: A product with no label cannot be matched to a safety data sheet, so no one knows what protection it needs. Reporting it lets it be identified or removed.

options.text: Smell the liquid to figure out what it is, and use it if it smells like cleaner.
options.why: Smelling an unknown liquid can itself be harmful, and many hazardous products smell like harmless ones.
options.misconception: I can identify a product by smell.

options.text: Try it on a small hidden spot first, and use it more widely if nothing seems to happen.
options.why: A small test does not tell you what the product is or what it does with other materials or over time.
options.misconception: If nothing happens right away, it is safe.

options.text: Pour it into a properly labeled bottle so that nobody else is confused about what it is.
options.why: Labeling a liquid when you do not know what it is makes it look known and safe, which is more dangerous.
options.misconception: A label makes a product safe to use.

templates.principle: Do not use an unlabeled product; report it so it can be identified with its label and safety data sheet.

review.notes: Workplace SDS availability stated in scenario; no regulatory claims.

templates.scenario: This spill clean-up procedure is posted at {workplace|the}.
templates.prompt: Tap the step that is a problem.

segments.whyFine: Wearing protective gloves is a sensible first step.

segments.text: Take away the wet floor sign before you start cleaning so it is not in your way.
segments.why: Removing the warning sign before the spill is cleaned leaves others unaware of the hazard.

segments.text: Clean up the spill using the supplies provided.
segments.whyFine: Cleaning the spill is the goal of the procedure.

segments.text: Place the wet floor sign back until the floor is completely dry.
segments.whyFine: Keeping the warning in place until the floor is dry protects others.

templates.principle: Keep warnings in place until a hazard is gone; never remove them early to make work easier.

review.notes: Single step removes the warning too early.

templates.scenario: At {workplace|the}, {coworker} has a small cut and has put on a bandage, but a little blood is on a counter. Employees at your workplace are trained to treat all blood as potentially infectious. Gloves and disinfectant are provided, and your {lead} is nearby.

options.text: Put on gloves, clean the counter with the provided disinfectant as trained, and dispose of the materials properly.
options.why: Treating all blood as potentially infectious, and using the protection and steps you were trained on, protects you and others.

options.text: Keep people away from the counter and ask your {lead} to arrange for it to be cleaned.
options.why: This keeps others safe, but you were trained and equipped to handle it, so waiting leaves the hazard in place longer.
options.misconception: Specialized situations are always for someone else.

options.text: Wipe it up quickly with a paper towel and throw it in the regular trash, since it is such a small amount.
options.why: A small amount can still be infectious, and bare hands and ordinary disposal skip the precautions you were trained to use.
options.misconception: A small amount is not a risk.

options.text: Ask {coworker} to wipe up the counter without gloves, since it was {coworker}'s own blood.
options.why: Contact with blood is a risk even from your own cut, and asking an injured person to clean it adds risk and ignores the precautions.
options.misconception: Your own blood is not a risk to you.

templates.principle: Treat all blood as potentially infectious: use protective equipment and the procedures you were trained on.

review.notes: Training and supplies are stated; no medical or legal claims beyond the scenario.
